newsitem.title: USA: Hundreds gather for pro-Tibet rally in New York.
newsitem.headline: Hundreds gather for pro-Tibet rally in New York.

text.p: Hundreds of supporters of Tibet gathered on Monday at a rally near the United Nations, where Nobel laureate Jose Ramos-Horta urged the crowd to keep alive the cause of Tibetan autonomy.
Autonomy for Tibet is not only a moral issue but a strategic one for Asian nations, Ramos-Horta said in a speech to mark Tibetan National Uprising Day.
With its history, religion and traditions, "Tibet could play a major role in peace-making, peace-building, conflict resolution" in the region, he said.

Ramos-Horta, an East Timor resistance leader now living in exile, and Bishop Carlos Belo were awarded the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize for their efforts to bring peace to the former Portugese colony of East Timor, invaded by Indonesia in 1975 and annexed the next year in a move never recognised by the United Nations.
Ramos-Horta warned the crowd of about 200 gathered for the rally and a march to the Chinese mission not to accept the "fait accompli of brute force."

Chinese troops occupied Tibet in 1951 and suppressed a rebellion in the mountainous region in 1959 that forced Tibet's spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, and thousands of followers to seek exile in India.
"What's happening here today is a tribute, evidence of how the Tibetan people have succeeded," Ramos-Horta said.
Police said 16 people later were arrested for disorderly conduct and issued a summons for sitting down in the street in front of the Chinese mission.
Ramos-Horta played down suggestions that changes in the Chinese leadership after the recent death of Deng Xiaoping would help the Tibetan cause.

"I don't think the death of Deng Xiaoping means really much in terms of a turning point," he said. "What is a turning point is that the Chinese Communist leadership has lost completely any legitimacy to be in power.
"Today the Chinese leadership is no different from a fascist dictatorship," he said.
A spokesman for the Dalai Lama told the rally he hoped China would be amenable now to opening up a dialogue on the future of Tibet.
In Washington, Vermont's two U.S. senators urged China to release a Tibetan filmmaker who was sentenced last December to 18 years in prison on spy charges.

Sens. Patrick Leahy, a Democrat, and James Jeffords, a Republican, said there was no evidence to support the charges against Ngawang Choephel, a student at Middlebury College in Vermont in 1993 and 1994.

"I was outraged when I learned of Mr. Choephel's 18-year prison sentence in December, after a secret trial and over a year of incommunicado detention. The Chinese government has not released a shred of evidence that Mr. Choephel committed any crime," Leahy said in a Senate speech.

Choephel and his family fled Tibet for India in 1968. He returned to Tibet in July 1995 to prepare a documentary film about Tibetan performing arts and was arrested the following month. He was charged with espionage in October 1996.
Leahy and Jeffords are co-sponsoring a Senate resolution calling on China to release Choephel and other prisoners of conscience in Tibet immediately.
